questions_and_answers.question_text: What is lǚguǎn the general term for?
What may follow lǚguǎn when it comes after a verb or after zài?
Which other kinds of place word behave the same way?
What is yàoshi an alternate word for?
What does the ending -hǎo le indicate?
Write the Chinese for "He stayed in this hotel for two months" in both acceptable forms.

answers.answer_text: Tā zài zhèige lǚguǎnli zhùle liǎngge yuè, or Tā zài zhèige lǚguǎn zhùle liǎngge yuè.
To have come to an agreement about something — it has been agreed on.
To have reached a conclusion about something — it has been thought out.
To have finished doing something — it has been finished.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Is the locational ending -li required after lǚguǎn?

answers.answer_text: No — there may be no locative ending at all.

articles.text:
Notes on Additional Required Vocabulary

8.  -hǎo le          to be satisfactorily completed
9.  lǚguǎn           hotel
10. shuōhǎo le       to have come to an agreement (about something);
                     (something) has been agreed on
11. xiǎnghǎo le      to have reached a conclusion (about something);
                     (something) has been thought out
12. yàoshi           if (alternate word for rúguǒ)
13. zuòhǎo le        to have finished doing (something);
                     (something) has been finished

Lǚguǎn is the general term for any kind of hotel. When following a verb or the prepositional verb zài, lǚguǎn may be followed by the locational ending -li, "in," or there may be no locative ending. This is also the case with other place words naming institutions, business establishments, and organizations.

Tā zài zhèige lǚguǎnli (OR       He stayed in this hotel for two
zài zhèige lǚguǎn) zhùle         months.
liǎngge yuè.
